## Overview

The Kavango people, also known as the *vaKavango* or *haKavango*, are a Bantu ethnic group living on the Namibian side of the Namibian–Angolan border along the Kavango River. They are mainly riverine people, although about 20% live in the dry inland. Their livelihoods are based on fishery, livestock-keeping, and cropping, especially pearl millet. The Kavango Region of Namibia is named after them. Traditional political organization includes five kingdoms—Kwangali, Mbunza, Shambyu, Gciriku, and Mbukushu—each headed by a *hompa* or *fumu*, terms meaning “king.” The Kavango are matrilinear, and their most common language is RuKwangali.

## Material culture

### Architecture

Kavango kitchens are built outside the house and are called *masuga*; their roofs are mainly thatched.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources identify the harvest season in April as a seasonal context for the vakwangali, who eat *mafumpura*, a tuber-like plant dug from the soil when it starts to crack.

## Foodways

Kavango livelihoods include fishery, livestock-keeping, and cropping, mainly pearl millet. Pearl millet porridge is their staple food, and pearl millet is also used to make a fermented drink. During the harvest season in April, the vakwangali eat *mafumpura*, a tuber-like plant dug from the soil when the soil starts to crack.

## Language & religion

The Kavango languages are a group of Bantu languages known as Kavango–Southwest Bantu languages. The most common language spoken by the Kavango people is RuKwangali, used in Kwangali and Mbunza territory; Shambyu, Gciriku, and Mbukushu are also spoken in their corresponding territories. The sources classify Kavango as K30 and identify Gciriku as Manyo. Mbukushu, Luyana, and Yeyi are described as more divergent Bantu lineages. The religion of the Kavango people is mainly Christian, although traditional elements continue to have a place. Traditional law remains in use and is legitimized by the Namibian constitution.
